title: File Handling and I/O: Programs That Remember

questions.question: What does the Python statement `open("data.txt", "w")` do to an existing data.txt file?
options: Reads it and leaves it unchanged
Raises an error if the file exists
questions.rationale: Mode "w" truncates the file to zero length before writing — existing content vanishes. To preserve content use "a" (append), and to guard against accidental creation use "x", which errors if the file exists.

questions.question: The primary benefit of opening files with the `with` statement is:
options: It automatically closes the file even if an exception occurs
It compresses the file on disk
It loads the entire file into memory
questions.rationale: `with open(...) as f:` guarantees close() on scope exit — exceptions included. This flushes buffers, releases file handles, and avoids the data loss and leaks of manual close() management.

questions.question: To scan a 10 GB log file line by line without exhausting memory, the correct choice is:
options: f.seek(0) in a while loop with read()
questions.rationale: Iterating the file object streams lazily — only the current line occupies memory. read() and readlines() load the entire file at once, which for a 10 GB log is a guaranteed crash.

questions.question: Which mode is right for adding new entries to a running application's log file?
questions.rationale: Append mode places the cursor at end-of-file and preserves existing content — every run adds history. Mode "w" would erase yesterday's logs on each start, and "r" cannot write at all.

questions.question: f.write("hello") in Python:
options: Writes exactly hello with no newline
Fails if the file contains data
questions.rationale: write() writes the bytes you give it, nothing more — no newline is appended. The classic bug is writing several strings that end up glued on one line; either add \n yourself or use print(..., file=f).

questions.question: Images and PDFs must be opened in which mode?
questions.rationale: Non-text files contain arbitrary byte sequences that text mode's decoding and newline translation would corrupt. Binary modes pass bytes through untouched — the safe choice for every non-text format.

questions.question: Which module is the standard choice for saving a dictionary as a web-friendly file?
questions.rationale: json.dump() writes the dictionary as portable JSON text that any language and browser can read. pickle serialises Python objects too, but its files are Python-only and unsafe from untrusted sources.

questions.question: Reading a missing file raises which exception?
questions.rationale: open() in read mode raises FileNotFoundError when the path does not exist. Related I/O failures include PermissionError and UnicodeDecodeError — all worth catching explicitly around file operations.

questions.question: Buffering means:
options: Files are read twice for safety
Writes accumulate in memory before being flushed to disk
The file is copied to a temporary folder
questions.rationale: Writes land in an in-memory buffer, which is flushed to disk when full, when flush() is called, or when the file closes. This is why skipping close() can lose data — the buffer never reached the disk.

questions.question: Why is `Path("data") / "results.json"` preferred over string concatenation for paths?
options: It works identically across Windows and Unix separators
It reads the file as well
questions.rationale: pathlib's / operator joins path components using the current operating system's separator, avoiding the hard-coded \ or / bugs that break ported scripts. It also offers exists(), read_text(), and friends.
